weaknesses.title: NoSQL Injection — in authentication logic (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: The email parameter may be used directly in a NoSQL query without proper sanitization, allowing query manipulation.

weaknesses.title: SQL Injection — in authentication logic (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: If the backend uses SQL for user lookup, the email parameter could be used to manipulate queries if unsanitized.

weaknesses.title: Command Injection — via unexpected shell invocation (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: Backend systems may invoke shell commands using user input for debugging, logging, or integration, risking injection.

weaknesses.title: Unicode Injection — to bypass email validation or matching (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: The use of Unicode confusables in the email might trick the backend into misidentifying the target account.

weaknesses.title: NoSQL Injection — name parameter may be embedded unsafely into a MongoDB-like query forming an exploitable injection sink (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
weaknesses.rationale: The `name` parameter is likely used in database lookups, and if the backend is using NoSQL (such as MongoDB) with unsafe query construction, malicious operators like `$ne` or `$regex` injected in `name` could manipulate the query logic.

weaknesses.title: Unicode Injection — name parameter may accept non-ASCII characters leading to inconsistent encoding handling across systems (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
weaknesses.rationale: If the application doesn't normalize or properly reject Unicode inputs in `name`, it could cause discrepancies in record matching, logging, or access control decisions due to different UTF representations.

weaknesses.title: Authentication Bypass — via missing or spoofed session ID (`sid`) in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: If the application does not properly validate the `sid` or relies on predictable/sessionless initiation, unauthorized users might establish unauthorized connections or access restricted channels.

weaknesses.title: Account Takeover — via email enumeration or weak login validation (param `email`, param `password`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: The login endpoint may reveal account existence or allow brute-force attempts leading to unauthorized access.

weaknesses.title: LDAP Injection — if LDAP-backed auth is used (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: Email parameter could be leveraged to inject LDAP search filters if backend binds to LDAP without input sanitization.

weaknesses.title: IDOR — name parameter may be used directly to query internal challenge objects without proper ownership checks (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
weaknesses.rationale: User-controlled `name` value is passed to the API endpoint which may retrieve internal challenge records directly by name without validating if the requesting user should have access to them.

weaknesses.title: SSRF via Transport Parameter — exploiting `transport=polling` in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: If the server uses the `transport` parameter value to determine backend communication methods without sanitization, it might initiate unintended outgoing requests, potentially leading to internal network scanning or resource access.

weaknesses.title: SSRF — URL Parameter `transport` (GET /socket.io/)
weaknesses.rationale: The `transport` parameter could instruct the server to initiate unintended outbound connections.

weaknesses.title: Prototype Pollution — via query parameters (`EIO`, `transport`, `t`, `sid`) in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: Socket.IO implementations in Node.js may improperly handle user-supplied keys like `__proto__` or `constructor` through query parameters, leading to prototype pollution which could affect application logic or lead to XSS.

weaknesses.title: Denial of Service (DoS) via malformed polling data — sending invalid payload `"40"` in body of POST to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: Improper parsing of the fixed body content “40” may crash or stall the server’s Socket.IO engine if it expects structured data but receives unexpected input.

weaknesses.title: Parameter Pollution — via duplicated or conflicting query parameters (`EIO`, `transport`, `t`, `sid`) in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: Injecting duplicate or malformed parameters may confuse the Socket.IO parser or backend logic, causing unpredictable behavior or exposing debug functionality.

weaknesses.title: Heap-Based Buffer Overflow — via excessively long values in query parameters (`t`, `sid`) in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: Native or poorly handled string processing of long untrusted inputs in C++ addons or underlying libraries could overflow buffers, crashing or compromising the service.

weaknesses.title: Logging Injection/Evasion — via non-printable or encoded characters in the `t` or `sid` parameters in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: If these parameters are logged verbatim without sanitization, malicious encodings could corrupt logs or hide malicious activity from detection systems.

weaknesses.title: JSON Injection — via malformed JSON body (body `{"email": "...", "password": "..."}`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: The application may improperly parse or reflect values from the JSON body, leading to injection or parsing errors.

weaknesses.title: Brute Force / Rate Limit Bypass — on password parameter (param `password`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: The login endpoint might not enforce rate limiting, enabling credential stuffing or brute force attacks.

weaknesses.title: Password Reset Logic Abuse — if login triggers resets or hints (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
weaknesses.rationale: Some systems auto-trigger resets or reveal hints upon failed logins, which could lead to account takeover.

weaknesses.title: Parameter Pollution — URL Parameters (`EIO`, `transport`, `t`, GET /socket.io/)
weaknesses.rationale: Duplicated or manipulated parameters could alter Socket.IO handshake or routing behavior.

weaknesses.title: Cache Deception — URL Parameter `t` (GET /socket.io/)
weaknesses.rationale: The `t` parameter, often used for cache busting, could be abused to trick the server into caching sensitive responses under public URLs.

weaknesses.title: Parameter Pollution — name parameter may be duplicated or combined with other params to confuse backend parsing logic and bypass restrictions (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
weaknesses.rationale: Adding multiple `name` parameters or combining `name` with other unexpected parameters could lead to inconsistent processing between frontend/backend or WAF/API, potentially bypassing filters or altering query behavior.

weaknesses.title: XSS — Reflected Payloads via `EIO` or `transport` Parameters (GET /socket.io/)
weaknesses.rationale: These parameters might be reflected in error messages or debug responses without sufficient sanitization, enabling cross-site scripting.

weaknesses.title: XSS — name parameter may be reflected or stored unsafely in HTML responses leading to script execution (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
weaknesses.rationale: The `name` value is provided by the user and may be rendered in HTML context either immediately (reflected) or later (stored), especially on result pages or UI components, potentially enabling cross-site scripting attacks.

weaknesses.title: Open Redirect — name parameter might be used in redirection logic without validation if the API endpoint handles redirects or callbacks (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
weaknesses.rationale: Although not obvious from the path, if the response includes any form of dynamic redirect based on the `name` value (e.g., after processing), it might allow crafting arbitrary destination URLs.

weaknesses.title: WebSocket Session Manipulation — via session ID (`sid`) parameter in POST request to `/socket.io/`
weaknesses.rationale: The `sid` parameter identifies an existing WebSocket session; manipulating it could allow hijacking or interfering with active sessions if insufficient validation occurs server-side.

weaknesses.title: WebSockets Misconfiguration — Upgrade Path via `/socket.io/` endpoint (GET /socket.io/)
weaknesses.rationale: The Socket.IO endpoint may insecurely handle polling-to-WebSocket upgrades, enabling hijacking or data leakage.
